title: Practice makes portable!
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck takes a close look at a 2023 study by Mancenido et al. comparing three approaches to teacher professional development: traditional reading and discussion, practice-based work with video decomposition and rehearsal, and a mixed approach without rehearsal. Practice-based and mixed groups did equally well on written vignette responses and both beat the traditional group, but only practice-based training produced the best performance in a simulated classroom with actors. What he finds most interesting is that teachers who had only practised the correct-answer scenario did just as well when the simulated students gave incorrect answers, suggesting rehearsal can prepare teachers for unexpected events. He draws two lessons: plan rehearsal around problems teachers actually face, and use rehearsal to build judgement about when and how to use a technique, not merely to close a knowing-doing gap. He urges coaches to look at the situation instead of looking for the technique, illustrating with a cold-call example in which a teacher wisely names the student first.
points: Practice-based training outperformed reading and discussion on both written vignettes and the simulated classroom task, and only it improved execution.
Teachers who rehearsed only the correct-answer situation handled incorrect student answers equally well, hinting that rehearsal transfers to unexpected events.
Rehearsal should target the real recurring problems teachers script for themselves, so any improvement also solves an ongoing difficulty.
Treating rehearsal as closing a knowing-doing gap reflects a deficit model, because experienced teachers more often need help with judgement about when to use a technique.
Coaches should look at the situation and not just for the technique, since knowing when not to use cold call is as skilful as knowing when to use it.
quotes: The researchers compared how well the three different groups performed in the practice task and found that the practice-based training group performed the best, by quite some distance.
This is super interesting because they performed just as well when confronted with incorrect answers as they did when confronted with correct answers.
It suggests that rehearsal is potentially powerful for helping teachers develop their responses to unexpected events (the unexpected incorrect answer).
We should also make sure that this rehearsal focuses on situations that teachers will actually find themselves in.
They are, much more often, at the stage where they need professional learning to help them improve their judgement about when and how to use the technique.
This isn’t a failure on the teacher’s part. Mastering cold call is as much about knowing when not to use it as it is about knowing when to use it.
We can only do it if we are looking at situational judgement.
Knowing when not to use the technique and when to adapt it is just as important as knowing when to use it
